abstract: AI agents can now do more work than people can continuously supervise. Many systems add logs, guardrails, approvals, and orchestration, yet still let one agent act, report what happened, interpret the rule, and gain authority. Putting a human in the loop doesn’t create governance when the system can manufacture the case for its own authority. That’s self-certification followed by ceremonial approval. We offer a practical alternative: agents act; trusted systems remember; rules authorize; people govern. These functions separate work, evidence, authority, and responsibility. The central integrity rule is that an agent receiving new authority must not be able to manufacture all the evidence sufficient to receive it. Governed processes decide what’s allowed now from current facts about the object, environment, dependencies, identity, policy, and time—rather than from completed steps alone. Rules turn competent evidence into narrow, expiring, revocable capabilities enforced where action becomes real. People step in when judgment, responsibility, exception, or risk requires accountable human authority and a genuine veto. This architecture applies at consequential boundaries without turning every agent action into a human approval task.

figures.title: Four offices of governed agency
transcript: Work becomes consequential only through evidence, scoped authority, and accountable government.
the action cannot become real without the grant
Functions may share technology. Their powers must remain legible.
relationships: The main chain runs from Agents act to Systems remember to Rules authorize to People govern.
Rules authorize feeds the enforcement point; People govern feeds it through a distinct exception or accountable-decision path.
The enforcement point prevents the proposed action from becoming real without a grant.

figures.title: Self-certification isn’t governed autonomy
transcript: The log is inside the same control boundary
Component count does not create governance. Control boundaries do.
relationships: The one-effective-actor panel cycles through Act, Report, Proceed, and Judge inside one control boundary; its log is inside that boundary.
The separated-authority panel runs Actor to independently governed Evidence to a Versioned rule to Enforcement checked at commit time.

figures.title: Evidence becomes scoped authority
transcript: A governed transition issues a capability—not a vague status.
Execution and outcome return as new evidence
Permission is where facts become power.
relationships: Proposal identifies the exact object; Observe supplies attributed facts; Verify checks fresh, competent evidence; Rule identifies a named version; Grant binds the principal, object, operation, invalidators, evidence digest, expiry and use conditions; Commit checks and enforces.
Execution and outcome return from Commit to Observe as new evidence.

figures.title: Put people where human authority changes the decision
transcript: Put people where human authority changes the decision
current evidence • explicit rule • narrow grant • unavoidable enforcement
People don’t repeat the machine’s work. They decide the part that remains legitimately human.
relationships: The ordinary machine-verifiable path leads to authorized action without ceremonial approval.
Judgment, Responsibility, Exception, and Risk connect to that path as separate human-governance triggers.
The Decision packet contains facts and provenance, uncertainty and options, impact and reversibility, and a real veto with an owner.

figures.title: One software change: normal flow, invalidation, and recovery
transcript: One software change: normal flow, invalidation, and recovery
old test stays true; grant dies
A mature process knows how authority disappears.
relationships: The normal software-change path runs Agent to Build to Validate to Rule P17 to Merge to Deploy.

Dependency changes invalidate validation: the old test stays true and the grant dies. A compromised validator loses source competence. Grant replay or bypass is denied and produces a security record at Merge.
Recovery choices are deny, revalidate, narrow, escalate, and rollback; a mature process knows how authority disappears.
